summary: Defines YANG, a data modeling language for configuration and state data that NETCONF manipulates, as well as for NETCONF remote procedure calls and notifications. It lets network device settings be described in a precise, machine-readable way.

plainLanguage.summary: Network devices have many settings. YANG is a way to write a clear blueprint of every setting and its allowed values so tools can read and check them.

questions: yang data modeling language for netconf
what is the difference between yang and netconf
how do you update a yang module
subtitle: The language for writing down exactly what configuration, state, operations and notifications a NETCONF device offers.

tldr.problem: NETCONF can carry any XML, so client and server need a precise, shared description of what data and operations a device really has, and what values are valid.
tldr.mechanism: YANG describes that data as a tree of modules made of containers, lists, leafs and typed values, plus RPCs, notifications, constraints, optional features and rules for evolving a module. The RFC also defines how each model maps to NETCONF XML.
tldr.outcome: A YANG module becomes a contract between NETCONF client and server. RFC 6020 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9890.

facts.label: Models
facts.value: NETCONF configuration, state, RPCs and notifications

today: RFC 6020 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2010, and it is updated by RFC 9890. It has not been obsoleted according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: What YANG Is For
sections.content:
YANG is a data modeling language used to model configuration and state data manipulated by the Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF), NETCONF remote procedure calls (RPCs) and NETCONF notifications. It describes the operations and content layers of NETCONF.

The RFC covers the syntax and semantics of the language, how a model is represented in XML, and how NETCONF operations are used to manipulate the data. A YANG module defines a hierarchy of data, which allows a complete description of all data sent between a NETCONF client and server.

The design is deliberately narrow. YANG limits itself to NETCONF data models, not arbitrary XML documents or arbitrary data models. It strikes a balance between high-level data modeling and low-level encoding, so a reader of a module can see the high-level view while understanding how the data will look in NETCONF operations. To the extent possible it stays compatible with SNMP's SMIv2, and SMIv2-based MIB modules can be automatically translated into YANG for read-only access. Reverse translation is not a goal.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a toy with many switches. YANG is the instruction sheet that says which switches exist and what each can be set to, written so both people and computers can read it.

sections.title: The Building Blocks of a Model
sections.content:
YANG models data as a tree in which each node has a name and either a value or a set of child nodes. Four kinds of node do most of the work.

  • A leaf holds one value of a particular type and has no children, for example host-name of type string.
  • A leaf-list is a sequence of leafs, each with exactly one value of one type, such as a list of domain names to search.
  • A container groups related nodes in a subtree. It has child nodes and no value.
  • A list defines a sequence of entries, like records. Each entry is uniquely identified by the values of its key leafs, set with the key statement. The key statement MUST be present if the list represents configuration.

A container can optionally carry a presence statement. Then the mere existence of the container is itself configuration, like an ssh container whose presence means SSH is enabled. A container without it exists only to organize data.

Each node maps to XML in a direct way: a node becomes an element named after its identifier, in the module's namespace. A list entry is a repeated element with its key leafs first. A unique statement can add a further rule that combinations of leaf values must not repeat across entries.

The choice and case statements describe alternatives that cannot appear together. Choice and case nodes appear only in the schema tree, not in the data tree or in NETCONF messages. The anyxml statement defines a node that can hold an unknown chunk of XML.
sections.plainLanguage: A leaf is one box with one thing in it. A container is a drawer holding several boxes. A list is a stack of identical forms, each with its own name written at the top so you can tell them apart.

sections.title: Modules, Submodules and Reuse
sections.content:
The module is the base unit of definition. A module defines a single data model, either a complete one or additions to an existing one. A module may be split into submodules, which contribute definitions to one module and belong to only one module. The outside view stays that of a single module.

A module reaches other modules with import and its own submodules with include. Imports can name a specific revision-date, so an importing module is unaffected when the imported module later publishes a new revision. Circular chains of imports or includes MUST NOT exist. Names from another module are used with a locally defined prefix, as in p:a. Every module also declares an XML namespace, and the namespace and prefix statements are required in a module.

Three mechanisms support reuse and extension:

  • typedef derives a new type from a built-in or another derived type.
  • grouping defines a reusable set of nodes that uses instantiates. The refine statement lets a use tailor some details, such as a description.
  • augment inserts new nodes into another place in the schema tree, in the same module or an external one. This is useful for vendors adding vendor-specific parameters to standard models. If the target is in another module, the added nodes MUST NOT be mandatory.

Typedefs and groupings may be nested and are scoped like names in a programming language. Names in a grouping are resolved where the grouping is defined, not where it is used. Only top-level types and groupings can be used outside their module.
sections.plainLanguage: Modules are chapters of a big manual. A grouping is a stamp you can press wherever you need the same set of boxes, and augment is a sticky note that lets someone else add a new page to your chapter.

sections.title: Syntax, Types and YIN
sections.content:
YANG syntax is similar to SMIng and to programming languages like C and C++. That C-like syntax was chosen for readability, since YANG values the time and effort of the readers of models above those of module writers and tool developers. Modules use UTF-8. Comments are C++ style, with // for a line and /* */ for a block. Statements end in a semicolon or hold a block in braces, and strings may be quoted with single or double quotes and joined with +. Identifiers are case sensitive and implementations MUST support identifiers up to 64 characters.

Values have built-in types: the integer types int8 to int64 and uint8 to uint64, decimal64, string, boolean, enumeration, bits, binary, leafref, identityref, empty, union and instance-identifier. A derived type can restrict a base type with range, length or pattern. For example, a percent typedef can be a uint8 with range 0 .. 100.

A few types carry their own rules. A decimal64 MUST have a fraction-digits statement with a value from 1 to 18. A leafref points at another leaf through a path, and the data is valid only if the referenced leaf exists. A leafref cannot be restricted, and circular chains of leafrefs are not allowed.

Finally, a YANG module can be translated into an equivalent XML syntax called YIN. The translation does not change the information content, so YIN can be round-tripped back into YANG, though comments and whitespace are not preserved. YIN lets developers use XML tools such as XSLT.
sections.plainLanguage: YANG is written a bit like a tidy computer program so that people can read it easily. Each box has a type, like a number or a word, and a type can have limits, like only numbers from 0 to 100.

sections.title: State, RPCs and Notifications
sections.content:
YANG models more than settings. The config statement separates the two kinds of data. A node with config true is configuration. It is returned by <get-config> and can be sent in <edit-config> or <copy-config>. A node with config false is state data. It is returned by <get> but not by <get-config>, and cannot be sent in an edit. The RFC's example is an interface with a configured speed and a read-only observed-speed. If no config is given, a node inherits it from its parent, and the top default is true.

The rpc statement defines a new NETCONF operation. Its name becomes the element name under the <rpc> element, and its parameters are modeled with input and output blocks using ordinary data definition statements. The RFC's example is an activate-software-image operation that takes an image-name and returns a status.

The notification statement models an event that a server can send. Its content is described with the same data definition statements, and the XML form is an eventTime followed by the notification element. The RFC's example is a link-failure notification carrying the interface name and its admin and operational status.

When a client edits configuration, it uses the operation attribute to merge, replace, create or delete a node. Creating data that already exists produces a data-exists error. Deleting data that does not exist produces data-missing.
sections.plainLanguage: Some knobs you can turn, and some are just dials you can only read, like a speedometer. YANG also lets you define new buttons to press and new alarms that ring when something happens.

sections.title: Constraints, Features and Deviations
sections.content:
A YANG model is a contract between client and server, and the strength of YANG lies in the strength of that contract. The RFC gives modelers three conformance mechanisms: the basic behavior of the model, optional features, and deviations.

Constraints keep data valid. The must statement holds an XPath expression that MUST evaluate to true, and its error-message and error-app-tag go into the <rpc-error>. The when statement makes a node valid only under a condition. Other constraints are mandatory, min-elements, max-elements, unique and leafref paths. For configuration data they MUST be enforced while parsing RPC payloads, while processing NETCONF operations, and during validation. For the running and startup datastores that validation happens at the end of an <edit-config> or <copy-config>. For the candidate datastore it waits for a <commit> or <validate>. Expressions are conceptually evaluated, so a device need not run an XPath engine.

Features mark parts of a model as optional. A feature statement names a capability, such as local-storage for syslog, and an if-feature statement ties nodes to it. Nodes tagged with a feature are ignored by a device that does not support it.

Deviations let a device say that it does not implement a model faithfully. A deviation targets a schema node and uses deviate with not-supported, add, replace or delete. The RFC strongly discourages them, says they MUST only be used as a last resort, and says they MUST never be part of a published standard.

A server advertises its modules in the NETCONF <hello> message. The capability is the module's namespace URI with parameters such as module, revision, features and deviations. A server MUST advertise all revisions of all modules it implements.
sections.plainLanguage: A model is a promise about how a device behaves. Some promises only apply if the device has a certain part, like a camera, and if a device cannot keep a promise it has to say so up front instead of surprising you later.

sections.title: Updating a Module Safely
sections.content:
Modules evolve, but changes are not allowed if they have any potential to cause interoperability problems between a client using an original specification and a server using an updated one. Every published change MUST add a new revision statement in front of the existing ones. The module name and the namespace MUST NOT change, and obsolete definitions MUST NOT be removed because other modules may still reference them.

The RFC lists what is allowed. Examples include adding new enums to an enumeration or new bits to a bits type without changing old values, widening a range, length or pattern, adding a default to a leaf that has none, relaxing a must, and adding new typedefs, groupings, RPCs, notifications, features and identities. New data nodes are allowed if they do not add mandatory nodes to existing places. A type may be swapped only if its syntax and meaning stay the same: an inline type can become a typedef, but int8 cannot become int16. A status may move from current to deprecated to obsolete.

Anything else that changes the meaning of an existing definition MUST be done with a new definition and a new identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: If you update the rules of a game, players who learned the old rules must not suddenly be wrong. So you can add new things and loosen rules, but if you want to change what something means, you give it a brand new name.

sections.title: Standard Error Responses
sections.content:
The RFC defines NETCONF error replies for model violations. If the relevant statement has an error-app-tag, that overrides the default. Each case sets an error-tag and an error-app-tag:

  • A violated unique constraint gives operation-failed with data-not-unique, and the error info lists the non-unique leafs.
  • Too many entries in a list or leaf-list gives operation-failed with too-many-elements, and too few gives too-few-elements.
  • A violated must gives operation-failed with must-violation.
  • A leafref or require-instance that points at nothing gives data-missing with instance-required.
  • A mandatory choice with no nodes gives data-missing with missing-choice.
  • An insert that names a non-existing instance gives bad-attribute with missing-instance.

During payload parsing, a value that violates its type returns an invalid-value error, missing list keys return missing-element, and data from more than one case of a choice returns bad-element.
sections.plainLanguage: When you fill in a form wrongly, the device does not just say no. It says which rule you broke, using agreed words, so your program can understand and react.

sections.title: IANA Registry and Media Types
sections.content:
RFC 6020 creates a registry named YANG Module Names for module and submodule names. For each entry it records the name, the assigned XML namespace and prefix for a module (or the parent module for a submodule), and a reference to the documentation. There were no initial assignments. Allocation requires RFC publication, names MUST be unique, and names and namespaces MUST each be unique across the registry. The prefix ietf- is reserved for IETF stream documents and irtf- for IRTF stream documents.

The RFC also registers two XML namespaces, urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:1 and urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:yin:1, and two media types: application/yang with the file extension .yang, and application/yin+xml with the extension .yin.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps a public phone book of module names so that no two people pick the same name, and it set up labels for the two file types, one for YANG files and one for YIN files.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the language itself has no security impact on the Internet, and that the same considerations apply as for base NETCONF. Data modeled in YANG, and RPCs or notifications defined in it, might carry sensitive information. Security issues belong to the use of that data, and are to be handled in documents about specific data models and about the interfaces, such as NETCONF, used to manipulate it.

That data depends on the security of the transmission infrastructure, the security of applications that store or release it, and adequate authentication and access control. The RFC adds that YANG parsers need to be robust against malformed documents. Reading malformed documents from unknown or untrusted sources could let an attacker gain the privileges of the user running the parser, and in an extreme case the whole machine could be compromised.
sections.plainLanguage: The language is just a way of writing things down, so it is not dangerous by itself. The care is needed in who may see or change the settings, and in not trusting strange files when you read them.
